q: What is URA’s mandate?
a: To assess, collect, and account for central government tax and non-tax revenue, and advise government on revenue policy.

q: What is URA’s mission?
a: Mobilize revenue for national development in a transparent and efficient manner.

q: What is URA’s vision?
a: A transformational revenue service for Uganda’s economic independence.

q: What is URA’s strategic direction?
a: Cultivate a taxpaying culture by providing reliable services, developing leadership, and building strategic partnerships.

q: What are URA’s core values?
a: Patriotism, Integrity, Professionalism.

q: What does Patriotism mean at URA?
a: Serving the nation with pride and building alliances with citizens who share commitment to Uganda and the agency.

q: What does Integrity mean at URA?
a: Consistently serving clients with impeccable conduct, transparency, honesty, reliability, and accountability to rules and regulations.

q: What does Professionalism mean at URA?
a: Executing roles with skill, ethics, courtesy, respect, and agility while avoiding bias and striving for excellence and collaboration.

q: What is URA’s Client Value Proposition?
a: Simplified, timely, reliable, and convenient revenue services everywhere at minimum cost to the client.

q: How does URA describe its culture?
a: Service-oriented and transformational; nurtures ethical, professional staff to deliver a delightful client experience in an enabling business environment.

q: Where is URA headquarters located?
a: Plot M193/M194, Nakawa Industrial Area, P.O. Box 7279, Kampala.

q: How can I contact URA?
a: Toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000; WhatsApp 0772 140 000; email services@ura.go.ug; visit URA offices or the website ura.go.ug.

q: What services does URA provide?
a: URA (Uganda Revenue Authority) is the country's central tax and customs authority. Core services include: taxpayer registration (instant TIN); domestic tax administration -- VAT, PAYE and employment income, corporation tax, rental income tax, capital gains tax, withholding tax, stamp duty, and small-business taxes; customs -- import/export clearance, valuation, and passenger baggage and cargo processing; EFRIS e-invoicing and Digital Tax Stamps; tax exemption and compliance support, including for NGOs and religious institutions; taxpayer education such as the Taxpayer Starter Pack and the annual Taxation Handbook; and online payments and account management through the URA web portal.

q: What is the advance tax on the transport sector and why was it introduced?
a: It simplifies tax payment for transport operators, raises revenue for road construction and maintenance, and widens the tax base. It is collected on motorcycles, passenger vehicles (PSVs/buses), and goods or freight vehicles with loading capacity above 2 tonnes.

q: Which vehicles must pay and who is responsible?
a: Owners of motorcycles, passenger vehicles, and goods/freight vehicles above 2 tonnes must pay. The vehicle owner is solely responsible for paying the advance income tax.

q: How do I determine the loading capacity for goods vehicles?
a: Use the logbook values: loading capacity = gross weight – net weight.

q: How much advance tax do I pay by vehicle type?
a: Goods vehicles above 2 tonnes: UGX 50,000 per tonne of loading capacity per year. Trailers: UGX 50,000 per tonne per year. Passenger vehicles (PSVs) and buses: UGX 20,000 per passenger seat per year. Motorcycles (boda boda): UGX 20,000 per year (licensed to carry one passenger).

q: Example: How is advance tax computed for a 7-tonne goods vehicle?
a: Multiply loading capacity by the rate: 7 tonnes × 50,000 = UGX 350,000 per year.

q: Example: How is advance tax computed for a 14-seat omnibus?
a: Multiply seats by the passenger rate: 14 seats × 20,000 = UGX 280,000 per year.

q: Example: How is advance tax computed for a 67-seat bus?
a: Multiply seats by the passenger rate: 67 × 20,000 = UGX 1,340,000 per year.

q: How much does a boda boda pay?
a: A motorcycle licensed to carry one person pays UGX 20,000 per year as advance income tax.

q: How do I pay the advance tax?
a: Steps: 1) Go to the URA website and choose Make a payment. 2) Click “Click here to make a payment.” 3) Select taxpayer details and enter vehicle details. 4) Select Tax Head → Advance Tax for Motor vehicles. 5) Enter payment details, choose mode (e.g., mobile money), complete the captcha, and submit to generate the payment slip.

q: How is the advance tax treated when filing income tax returns?
a: When filing your income tax return, deduct the advance income tax paid from the tax payable (it offsets your final income tax).

q: What is the Authorized Economic Operator (AEO) program?
a: A trade facilitation initiative based on the WCO SAFE Framework where compliant traders partner with URA Customs to secure the supply chain and receive simplified, preferential clearance.

q: Who is an AEO?
a: Any individual, business, or government department involved in international trade that the Commissioner Customs authorizes after meeting supply chain security requirements.

q: Who are the prospective AEO clients?
a: Manufacturers (export/import), customs clearing agents, bonded warehouse keepers, importers and exporters, transporters and freight forwarders.

q: What are the objectives of the Uganda AEO scheme?
a: Promote and reward good business practices; strengthen Customs–business and Customs–Customs partnerships; foster inter-agency cooperation; secure the international supply chain; and encourage voluntary compliance with customs laws.

q: What is the eligibility criteria for becoming an AEO?
a: Be in international trade; able to use URA systems (e.g., ASYCUDA, e-tax); have at least 3 years of good compliance history; be financially sound (not bankrupt); implement the AEO Compliance Program.

q: What are the steps to attain AEO status?
a: 1) Write an expression of interest to Commissioner Customs. 2) Hold preliminary consultation with the Customs AEO team. 3) Submit the self-assessment form with supporting documents. 4) Customs vets the application and documents. 5) Customs conducts on-site inspection of premises. 6) If requirements are met, Commissioner Customs authorizes AEO status.

q: What are the immediate benefits of the AEO program to business?
a: Pre-arrival clearance; major clearance time reductions; priority treatment with Customs; choice of examination place; automatic renewal of licenses (agency/bonded warehouse); withholding tax exemption; priority in URA activities; secured parking at URA Tower; participation in AEO national working group.

q: What are the long-term benefits to business?
a: Lower cost of doing business; enhanced reputation; higher turnover; improved service quality; trusted/compliant profile; stronger internal controls; mutual recognition opportunities.

q: What is the Regional AEO program in the EAC?
a: An EAC-wide AEO framework running alongside the national program to boost revenue and trade facilitation, strengthen Customs–business partnerships, and secure the regional/global supply chain.

q: How can a Ugandan AEO operate outside Uganda (Mutual Recognition)?
a: Through Mutual Recognition Arrangements where partner countries recognize each other’s AEO programs (aligned to WCO SAFE), granting benefits to each other’s AEOs bilaterally or multilaterally.

q: What facilitation benefits do Regional AEO importers/exporters/manufacturers receive?
a: Expedited processing and automatic passing of declarations; no physical/document exams except random/risk-based with priority handling and choice of exam location; priority refund processing; consideration for reduced customs security where applicable.

q: What benefits do Regional AEO Customs Agents receive?
a: Guaranteed renewal of the agent’s license (payment still required); first priority to join new Customs initiatives; priority treatment in cargo clearance; waiver of movement bond when importer/exporter, agent, and transporter are all AEOs.

q: What benefits do Regional AEO Warehouse Operators receive?
a: Privilege to self-manage bonded warehouses (subject to law/conditions); guaranteed renewal of warehouse operator license (fees still due); consideration for reduced customs security on a case-by-case basis.

q: How are AEO consignments verified under special circumstances?
a: AEO importers are blue-lane: risk addressed via post-import audit; exams only on risk-based selection, and managers ensure AEOs receive priority even during system challenges.

q: What are business records?
a: Documents that capture a business’s transactions—income received and expenses paid—kept in physical or electronic form to show what the business earned and spent.

q: What kind of records do I have to keep?
a: Keep income records (date, amount, source; invoices, receipts, contracts, cash-register tapes) and expense records (receipts/vouchers with date, seller/buyer details, description, amount). If no receipt is provided, note supplier name/address, date, amount, and transaction details yourself.

q: How often should I keep records?
a: Record every transaction as it happens. Maintain daily income and expense logs; keep duplicate deposit slips, bank statements, cancelled cheques, and separate records for each business. Computerized records must be clear and readable.

q: What happens if I don’t keep adequate records?
a: URA may determine income using other methods and may reduce deductible expenses if required information is missing.

q: Why is it important to keep records?
a: Helps you claim allowable deductions, distinguish business vs non-business or non-taxable income, know your financial position, budget and access financing, and avoid problems during URA audits.

q: What does the Tax Procedures Code Act (S15) require about records?
a: Keep records in English (physical or electronic); if using another language/currency, seek Commissioner General’s permission and translate on request. Retain records for five years after the tax period (or longer if proceedings are ongoing).

q: What are capital gains?
a: Profits from disposing non‑depreciable business assets (e.g., land/buildings), sale of shares, or commercial buildings (excludes trading stock and depreciable assets).

q: What is a business asset?
a: Any asset used or held for use in business, held for sale in business, or any asset of a partnership or company.

q: When is there a disposal for capital gains tax?
a: When an asset is sold, exchanged, redeemed, distributed, gifted, destroyed, lost, or partially disposed.

q: When are capital gains taxed?
a: In the year of income when the gain or loss is realized.

q: What is a capital loss?
a: A loss on disposal of non‑depreciable business assets, shares, or commercial buildings.

q: What happens when a capital loss is made?
a: Capital losses are deductible (allowed against income).

q: How is a capital gain or loss computed?
a: Gain/Loss = Disposal proceeds (consideration) – Cost base. Cost base is purchase price plus capital/incidental acquisition costs (including consideration in kind).

q: Is there a separate capital gains tax law in Uganda?
a: No. Capital gains are taxed under the Income Tax Act, included with business income (Section 18(1)(a)).

q: How are capital gains for an individual taxed?
a: Gains on business assets are added to business income and taxed at individual rates; gains on shares or commercial buildings are taxed as property income at applicable rates.

q: How are capital gains for a corporate entity taxed?
a: Gains on business assets, shares, or commercial buildings are added to gross income and taxed at the standard corporate rate (30%).

q: How to compute tax when a business asset is sold after 12+ months?
a: Index the cost base for inflation: Adjusted cost base = CB × CPID / CPIA (CPI at sale month / CPI immediately before acquisition). Taxable gain = Sale price – adjusted cost base; then apply tax rate.

q: Example: sale after 12+ months (land 10,000,000 bought Jun 2022, sold 25,000,000 Aug 2023; CPIA 153.25, CPID 181.67)
a: Adjusted cost base ≈ 11,854,486; taxable gain ≈ 13,145,514; tax at 30% ≈ 3,943,654 UGX.

q: How to compute tax when sold within 12 months?
a: No inflation adjustment: gain = sale price – original cost base. Example: 25,000,000 – 10,000,000 = 15,000,000; tax at 30% ≈ 4,500,000 UGX.

q: Which disposals are not recognized (no gain taxed, no loss allowed)?
a: Transfers between spouses; transfers between former spouses under divorce/separation; involuntary disposals re‑invested in same‑kind asset within one year; transmission to a trustee or beneficiary on death of the taxpayer.

q: What is the basis of corporation tax?
a: Resident companies are taxed on worldwide income; non-resident companies are taxed on Uganda-source income. Company income tax is called corporation tax.

q: What is the legal basis and rate of corporation tax?
a: Imposed by the Income Tax Act on persons with chargeable income. Standard company rate is 30% on chargeable (business) income for both resident and non-resident companies.

q: How is a company’s tax liability determined (example)?
a: Compute profits then apply 30%: Example figures—total revenue 239,000,000; production costs 34,000,000; admin costs 16,000,000; net profit (chargeable income) 189,000,000; tax at 30% = 56,700,000.

q: What is a customs offence?
a: Any breach or attempted breach of statutory/regulatory provisions under the EAC Customs Management Act (EACCMA); penalties vary by severity.

q: Who is a customs proper officer?
a: An officer whose duty/right is to require or perform acts under EACCMA.

q: When does a customs officer commit an offence?
a: If they solicit/receive unauthorized rewards or connive/agree to acts that defraud customs revenue.

q: What are offences in customs areas?
a: Unauthorized entry/exit; failure to leave when ordered; refusing search/detention of self or goods.

q: What are offences on arrival?
a: Landing at non-authorized place; departing unloading place without clearance; returning to partner state without authority while on foreign voyage.

q: Is boarding a vessel before the proper officer allowed?
a: No; offence punishable by a fine up to USD 250.

q: Is removing goods from a customs area without paying duty an offence?
a: Yes; goods liable to forfeiture.

q: Where must passengers disembark?
a: Only at commissioner-appointed places; otherwise it is an offence.

q: Can warehoused goods be delivered as stores?
a: Yes, for vessels ≥250 tons; misuse is an offence.

q: Is unauthorized access to a warehouse an offence? Penalty?
a: Yes; goods in warehouse are untaxed. Unlawfully taking warehoused goods: up to 2 years imprisonment or fine = 25% of dutiable value.

q: Offences for export entry?
a: Failing to enter cargo properly; lacking documentary evidence for goods in the entry.

q: Can export goods be discharged in a Partner State?
a: Not without written permission/conditions; otherwise goods are forfeitable.

q: Is deficiency or surplus in cargo an offence?
a: Yes; missing reported goods (deficiency) or extra unmanifested goods (surplus) both are offences; goods liable to forfeiture.

q: Deadline to deliver transire for coastwise/transfer goods?
a: Immediately; vessels ≥250 tons may deliver within 24 hours of arrival.

q: Must transit goods follow specific routes?
a: Yes; deviating from commissioner-approved routes is an offence.

q: Owner’s liability for offences by authorized agent?
a: Owner prosecuted as if they committed the offence.

q: Is manufacturing under bond without a licence an offence?
a: Yes; penalty up to USD 5,000 or ≤3 years imprisonment or both.

q: Can a bonded factory alter premises freely?
a: Alterations require prior commissioner permission after proper entry of buildings/rooms/plant.

q: Is removing goods from an EPZ/Freeport for home use without authority an offence?
a: Yes; fine USD 5,000 or 50% of goods’ value, whichever is higher.

q: Penalty for unauthorized access to customs IT system?
a: Individual: up to 2 years or fine ≤USD 5,000; corporate: fine ≤USD 25,000.

q: Other notable customs offences and penalties
a: Conspiracy against EACCMA (≤5 years); shooting/wounding/violent acts against customs (≤20 years); armed with weapon while offending (≤10 years); disguising while offending (≤3 years); obstructing/rescuing/throwing seized goods (various penalties); interfering with seals/locks (≤3 years or fine ≤USD 2,500); missing goods from sealed premises (owner liable: ≤5 years or fine 25% of value).

q: Penalty for committing an offence with violence/weapon/disguise?
a: Violence: ≤20 years; armed: ≤10 years; disguised: ≤3 years.

q: Penalty for removing/defacing customs seals?
a: Up to 3 years or fine ≤USD 2,500 or both.

q: What is inducing another to commit an offence? Penalty?
a: Procuring/inducing someone to commit/assist an offence; penalty up to 1 year.

q: Is warning an offender an offence? Penalty?
a: Yes; warning someone engaged in an offence: up to 2 years or fine ≤USD 2,500 or both.

q: Is assuming the character of an officer an offence?
a: Yes; impersonation punishable by up to 3 years imprisonment.

q: Penalties for smuggling-adapted vessels/vehicles?
a: Master of vessel <250 tons: fine ≤USD 7,000; master of vessel/aircraft ≥250 tons: fine ≤USD 10,000; person in charge of vehicle: fine ≤USD 5,000.

q: What is Customs value?
a: Value used to levy ad valorem duties; ad valorem duty is a percentage of value, while specific duties are fixed amounts per unit (e.g., per litre, weight, or item).

q: Are there international rules for Customs value?
a: Yes. WTO Members apply the Agreement on Customs Valuation (ACV) based on transaction value plus specific adjustments; domesticated in EACCMA Section 122 and its Fourth Schedule.

q: What are the Customs valuation methods under ACV?
a: Six methods applied sequentially (methods 4 and 5 can swap on importer request): transaction value; transaction value of identical goods; transaction value of similar goods; deductive value; computed value; fallback method.

q: What is the transaction value method?
a: Primary method: price actually paid or payable for goods sold for export to Uganda, adjusted per Article 8 for dutiable costs not in the invoice price.

q: What counts as price actually paid or payable?
a: Total payment to/for seller, including indirect payments or debt settlements. Excludes post-import construction/assembly, post-import transport, and local duties/taxes if separately identified.

q: Conditions to use transaction value?
a: No use/disposal restrictions; no undeterminable conditions affecting price; seller doesn’t receive later resale proceeds unless adjusted; buyer-seller relationship did not influence price.

q: Which imports lack an import transaction?
a: Free consignments (gifts/samples); goods on consignment for auction; goods under hire/lease; intra-company transfers without separate legal entities; imports by non-residents selling locally (including via proxies/e-commerce).

q: What documents substantiate transaction value?
a: Commercial: purchase order, pro forma, sales contract, packing list, invoice, receipt. Transport: bill of lading/airway bill, freight invoice/debit note, insurance documents. Financial: proof of payment (TT, bank draft/receipt, credit instruments). Regulatory: transit docs, certificates of origin, permits/analysis/fumigation/phytosanitary certificates.

q: What is the transaction value of identical goods?
a: Use previously accepted transaction value of identical goods (same in all respects, quality, reputation), exported at similar time, in similar quantities and commercial level.

q: What is the transaction value of similar goods?
a: Use accepted transaction value of similar goods (commercially interchangeable, like characteristics/materials), exported at similar time; adjust for quantity/commercial level; consider other producers only if none from same producer.

q: What is the deductive value method?
a: When earlier methods fail, base value on domestic selling price of imported/identical/similar goods at first commercial level after import (within set period), deducting specified costs.

q: What costs are deducted under deductive value?
a: Commissions or profit/general expenses; inland transport/insurance; customs duties and local taxes payable on the sale.

q: What is the computed value method?
a: Value = cost of materials/fabrication/labour + profit & general expenses typical for such exports + transport and related costs to port of import. Used only when earlier methods fail and transaction is direct with manufacturer.

q: What is the fallback method?
a: Use reasonable means consistent with ACV/GATT, applying Articles 1–6 flexibly (e.g., using sales within 120 days if 90-day data unavailable).

q: Is invoice price automatically the customs value?
a: Not necessarily; it can represent customs value only if all ACV conditions and required additions are satisfied.

q: Is freight part of customs value in Uganda?
a: Yes for sea/road imports from outside EAC (CIF basis). For air, customs value uses cost + insurance only (freight excluded).

q: What is the basis for declaring imported goods?
a: Sea/road: CIF to port of discharge (invoice cost + ocean freight + insurance). Air: cost + insurance to Entebbe.

q: Can Customs reject a declared value?
a: Yes. Customs may reject if not satisfied with accuracy after review and explanation.

q: Can an importer challenge Customs’ valuation?
a: Yes. ACV allows administrative and judicial appeal without penalty.

q: How to appeal a valuation decision?
a: Escalate to Manager DPC → Commissioner Customs → Commissioner General; further recourse to court if still dissatisfied.

q: Are advance rulings on valuation available?
a: Yes. Uganda issues advance rulings on valuation methods/criteria (per WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement).

q: Is transfer pricing acceptable for customs value?
a: Relationship alone isn’t grounds to reject; transaction value may be accepted if price not influenced (per ACV Article 1.2). Customs reviews MNE transfer prices accordingly.

q: Can valuation infringements be prosecuted?
a: Yes. Submitting wrong documents, falsifying information, or breaching customs laws can lead to criminal prosecution.

q: Does origin country change vehicle customs value?
a: No. Same valuation method applies regardless of source country.

q: How are used motor vehicles and other used articles valued?
a: Based on EAC Administrative Ruling on valuation of used goods (13 Dec 2013) under EACCMA; URA publishes predetermined values for declarations.

q: Categories of used vehicles?
a: Passenger carrying (cars, wagons, buses), goods carrying (lorries, vans, pickups), and special purpose (e.g., excavators, graders).

q: Key parameters influencing used vehicle value?
a: Make, model, chassis/frame model, body type, engine capacity/horsepower, year of manufacture, drive/fuel type and similar specs.

q: Why are the first five methods inapplicable to used vehicles?
a: Sales are idiosyncratic so no reliable transaction value/identical/similar data; deductive and computed methods fail due to lack of preceding values and manufacturing data.

q: How is a boarded-off vehicle valued on re-registration?
a: Use customs value at first import then depreciate: ≤1yr 30%, >1–2yr 45%, >2–3yr 60%, >3–4yr 70%, >4yr 75%; apply to original customs value (not statistical).

q: Where to get the used motor vehicle value guideline?
a: URA website A–Z Topics > Used Motor Vehicle Valuation Database (eventManagementController link provided by URA).

q: What is the Customs Document Processing Centre (DPC)?
a: Centralized Customs office handling documentary checks for all declarations.

q: When did DPC start?
a: Launched 24 Feb 2017; fully operational June 2017.

q: Where is DPC located?
a: URA Headquarters, Nakawa Inland Port (NIP) building.

q: Who are the key DPC stakeholders?
a: Importers/exporters, customs agents, bonded warehouse owners, MDAs (UNBS, NDA, MAAIF, Interpol, Ministry of Works, NFA, UCDA, etc.).

q: Why was DPC created?
a: To shorten processing time via online submission, increase transparency, enable real-time monitoring, improve communication, professionalism, productivity, and SOP enforcement.

q: What specialized units does DPC have?
a: Motor Vehicle Unit, Fuel Unit, Export Unit, and General Goods Unit.

q: Does DPC operate 24/7?
a: Yes, three shifts daily; third shift reduced during COVID-19.

q: How can clients access DPC?
a: Via URA Touchpoint, desk phones, face-to-face meetings, online meetings (Zoom/Teams), and the Electronic Single Window.

q: Can importers file declarations without customs agents?
a: Generally no; declarations in ASYCUDA are filed by licensed customs agents. Some compliant manufacturers may self-declare.

q: Which documents does DPC require for clearance?
a: Financial: proforma/sales/commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, proof of payment, C36. Transport: freight invoice, bill of lading/airway bill/rail note. Regulatory: PVOC/COC, NDA permit, phytosanitary cert, lottery/gaming import permit, India shipping bill, South Africa export entry.

q: Why doesn’t DPC rely solely on invoice price?
a: DPC uses transaction value when credible; if in doubt, it applies alternative valuation methods sequentially (2–6) per EACCMA Fourth Schedule.

q: How to appeal a DPC decision?
a: Appeal to Supervisor DPC → Manager DPC → Assistant Commissioner Field Services if still unsatisfied.

q: Is a special form needed to appeal?
a: No; submit via URA Touchpoint or hard-copy with grounds and supporting evidence.

q: What documents must international travelers present when entering Uganda?
a: Passport valid ≥6 months; appropriate visa (e-visa/embassy/visa-free or on-arrival where eligible); yellow fever vaccination certificate (over 1 year old travelers); COVID-19 PCR within 72 hours if required by current health rules; proof of onward/return ticket.

q: What documents are needed for a foreign company to register and operate in Uganda?
a: Certificate of incorporation; board resolution to register in Uganda; memorandum and articles of association; list of directors and secretary with details; registered office address in Uganda; recent audited financial statements; URA Tax Identification Number (TIN); trading licence; sectoral investment licence where applicable (UIA).

q: Which documents are required at the point of entry for goods?
a: Bill of Lading/Airway Bill (contract/receipt/title); insurance certificate; proforma invoice; commercial invoice; certificate of origin (for preference); permits for restricted goods; purchase order; packing list (contents/weights/measures); sales contract; evidence of payment (receipts/bank proof).

q: What is DTS?
a: Digital Tax Stamps are markings with security features and codes applied to gazetted goods/packaging so URA can track and trace production/imports and combat counterfeits.

q: What is the Digital Tracking Solution?
a: A track-and-trace platform that sends production/importation data for specified products to URA and UNBS in real time; it pairs tax stamps (URA) with conformity stamps (UNBS).

q: Who must use DTS?
a: Manufacturers and importers of gazetted excisable products (e.g., spirits, wines, other specified goods) must affix and activate digital tax stamps per URA requirements.

q: How do I register for DTS?
a: On the URA portal go to e-Services → Digital Tracking Solution → register as importer or manufacturer, then forecast/order stamp quantities and pay the stamp fees.

q: How do I get and affix stamps?
a: After payment, collect stamps from SICPA Uganda (Henley Business Park, Ntinda) for manual/paper stamping, or receive codes directly to your automated DTS line; authorized staff must present ID and company letter/stamp on pickup.

q: Can importers stamp abroad?
a: Yes. Importers may stamp at origin or manually at their registered premises in Uganda.

q: Do exports need DTS stamps?
a: No. Gazetted products for export are exempt from DTS stamping but must carry export evidence (counting, marking for export, certified customs export documents) and must not be sold locally.

q: What are setup requirements for automated manufacturers?
a: Register for DTS, provide space/power/network for DTS equipment, stamp applicator (for spirits/wines), ejection system, secure server room, broadband with dedicated IP, cabling, and secure storage for spares/consumables.

q: What are requirements for manual producers/importers?
a: Register for DTS and provide labor to manually affix stamps; ensure stamps are activated after affixing.

q: What are the benefits of DTS?
a: Track-and-trace through the supply chain, quick reports, improved records, easier VAT refunds/return filing, faster customs clearance for importers, reduced smuggling/counterfeit risk, fair competition, and consumer protection.

q: What are the penalties for non-compliance?
a: Failure to affix/activate stamps: penal tax = double tax due or UGX 50m (higher). Defacing/printing over a stamp: double tax due or UGX 20m. Possession of unstamped gazetted goods: double tax due or UGX 50m. Unauthorized dealing in stamps: double tax due or UGX 10m.

q: What are key roles for stakeholders?
a: Manufacturers/importers: install/use DTS on excisable goods. Distributors/stockists: handle only stamped gazetted products. Consumers: buy/consume only stamped goods.

q: Who can help with DTS issues?
a: URA support: toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000 or WhatsApp 0772 140 000.

q: What is the Digital Tracking Solution (DTS)?
a: A track-and-trace platform that sends production/import data for specified products to URA and UNBS; products are stamped with digital tax stamps (URA) and conformity stamps (UNBS).

q: What key DTS terms should I know?
a: Stamp applicator: device affixing paper stamps on production lines (spirits/wines). Ejection system: removes rejects from the line. Line enable: connection so DTS equipment receives production details from manufacturer equipment.

q: How do I acquire DTS?
a: Register online via URA e-services (Digital Tracking Solution) as importer/manufacturer; forecast/order and pay stamp fees (allowed business expense); after payment confirmation collect stamps (or codes auto-loaded on DTS machines). Recipient must show ID plus employer letter or company stamp on delivery notes. Importers may stamp at origin or manually at registered premises.

q: Where do I pick Digital Tax Stamps?
a: From SICPA Uganda Ltd, Henley Business Park, Ntinda Industrial Area (Kampala). Directions: from Nakawa–Naguru junction take Stretcher Rd ~1km, turn right at Shell Stretcher; Henley Business Park on right. Coordinates: 0.340632, 32.616436.

q: What are the requirements to use DTS?
a: Automated manufacturers: register; space for DTS equipment; stamp applicator (spirits/wines); line ejection; secure server room; network cabling; broadband with dedicated IP; clean power; space for spares/tools. Manual producers/importers: register and provide labour to manually affix stamps.

q: Do exports require DTS?
a: No stamps on gazetted products for export. Exports monitored by providing certified export documents, counting/recording, marking for export, accompanying goods with export docs to exit point; export goods must not appear on local market.

q: What are the benefits of DTS?
a: Track/trace specified goods through the chain; instant transaction reports; improved record keeping; easier VAT refunds and return filing; faster customs clearance for importers; reduced smuggling/dumping and counterfeit; fair competition; consumer protection.

q: What are the penalties for non-compliance with DTS?
a: Failure to affix/activate stamps: penal tax = 2x tax due or UGX 50m (higher). Defacing/printing over stamp: 2x tax due or UGX 20m (higher). Possession of unstamped gazetted goods: 2x tax due or UGX 50m (higher). Unauthorized acquisition/sale of stamp: 2x tax due or UGX 10m (higher).

q: What are the responsibilities of different parties?
a: Manufacturers/importers: install/use DTS on excisable goods. Consumers: buy/consume only stamped gazetted products. Distributors/agents/stockists: handle only stamped gazetted products.

q: What is EFRIS?
a: Electronic Fiscal Receipting and Invoicing Solution—a system that records business transactions in real time and shares them with URA, issuing e-invoices/e-receipts with FDN, verification code, and QR code.

q: Is EFRIS a tax?
a: No. It is a digital system for invoicing/receipting; it does not itself impose tax.

q: Who must use EFRIS?
a: All VAT-registered businesses are required to issue e-invoices and e-receipts through EFRIS.

q: What are the benefits of EFRIS?
a: Better bookkeeping and stock management, reduced loss of paper invoices, accurate transaction tracking, and easier compliance with VAT rules.

q: What is VAT?
a: Value Added Tax—an indirect tax on consumption applied to the value added to goods and services; VAT-registered businesses collect it from customers and remit to URA.

q: Are there penalties for not issuing e-invoices/e-receipts?
a: Yes. VAT-registered businesses that fail to issue e-receipts/e-invoices can face fines.

q: How does EFRIS help business owners?
a: It streamlines issuing receipts/invoices, frees time, improves compliance, and supports business growth by keeping records organized digitally.

q: What attitude does the story encourage in young readers?
