q: What is EFRIS?
a: Electronic Fiscal Receipting and Invoicing Solution (EFRIS) is URA’s real-time e-receipting/e-invoicing system using EFDs, e-invoicing, or system-to-system links as per the Tax Procedures Code Act 2014.

q: Who must use EFRIS?
a: It is mandatory for all VAT-registered taxpayers. The Commissioner may gazette additional taxpayers (B2B, B2G, B2C) who must issue e-receipts/e-invoices.

q: Is EFRIS optional for non-VAT taxpayers?
a: Yes, non-VAT taxpayers are encouraged to adopt EFRIS to enjoy the benefits, though not mandated unless gazetted.

q: How do I register for EFRIS?
a: On ura.go.ug → EFRIS → log in with TIN/password → receive OTP → select First time registration → choose e-invoicing and/or EFDs, add business locations → submit for URA approval.

q: What do I need to register?
a: A valid TIN and portal password, access to email/phone to receive OTP, internet connectivity, and (if system-to-system) the ability to set up the API link.

q: What is an e-invoice vs an e-receipt?
a: An e-invoice is issued by a VAT-registered taxpayer; an e-receipt is issued by a non-VAT taxpayer. Both are generated through EFRIS.

q: What unique features are on an e-invoice/e-receipt?
a: They include a fiscal document number, verification code, and QR code for authenticity and validation.

q: What devices or channels can I use?
a: Options include Electronic Fiscal Devices (EFDs), the web portal, desktop/mobile client, or system-to-system API integration.

q: What are the benefits of EFRIS?
a: Faster refund processing, future prefilled returns, reduced penalties from accurate filing, real-time transaction tracking, secure digital storage of tax invoices, and fairer tax assessments.

q: How does data reach URA?
a: When a transaction is initiated in EFRIS (via device, portal, or API), the details are transmitted to URA in real time to generate an e-receipt or e-invoice.

q: Who can help with EFRIS issues?
a: Contact URA support: toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000 or WhatsApp 0772 140 000.

q: Who is an employer and who is an employee?
a: Employer: person or entity paying remuneration. Employee: individual engaged in employment.

q: What counts as employment?
a: Position in another’s employment, company directorship, any remunerated position (contract/permanent/part-time), or holding/acting in public office.

q: What amounts comprise employment income?
a: Wages, salaries, leave pay, overtime, fees, commissions, gratuities, bonuses, allowances (travel, entertainment, utilities, cost of living, housing, medical), employer-paid personal expenses, benefits in kind, termination/change-of-terms payments, insurance premiums paid by tax-exempt employer for employee/dependents, employee share scheme gains (value of shares/options less any consideration), gains on disposal of share options, compensation for restrictive covenants.

q: Which employment gains are exempt/relieved?
a: Pension; employer-paid medical expenses; life insurance premiums paid by a taxable employer; allowances/reimbursements for official duties; meals/refreshments provided equally to all staff on employer premises; employer retirement-fund contributions (employee’s own contribution is taxable); value of share rights/options granted; Local Service Tax deductible before PAYE; de minimis benefits < UGX 10,000 per month; resident threshold first UGX 235,000/month tax-free; 25% of terminal benefits after ≥10 years’ service; passage costs for non-Ugandan recruited abroad; actual travel/accommodation/meal reimbursements while on duty.

q: What is a benefit in kind?
a: Any non-cash facilitation tied to employment (past/present/future) provided by employer, employer’s associate, or to an employee/associate. Examples: private use of company car, domestic staff, meals/entertainment, utilities, debt relief, low-interest loans, housing, property provided on non–arm’s-length terms.

q: How is private use of an employer motor vehicle taxed?
a: Benefit = (20% × market value when first provided × days available for private use ÷ days in year) – any employee payment.

q: How are domestic staff benefits valued?
a: Taxable benefit equals total pay to housekeeper/gardener/driver/chauffeur provided to the employee minus any employee contribution; security guard provision is not treated as a taxable benefit.

q: How are meal/refreshment and utility benefits valued?
a: Meals/refreshments/entertainment: cost to employer minus employee contribution. Utilities for residence: cost to employer minus employee contribution.

q: How are low-interest loan benefits valued?
a: If total loans exceed UGX 1,000,000 and interest is below statutory rate (Bank of Uganda discount rate at year start), benefit = interest at statutory rate minus interest actually paid.

q: What are the monthly PAYE rates for residents?
a: 0–235,000: 0; 235,001–335,000: 10% of excess over 235,000; 335,001–410,000: 10,000 + 20% of excess over 335,000; above 410,000: 25,000 + 30% of excess over 410,000; above 10,000,000: add 10% of the amount exceeding 10,000,000. Non-residents have no 235,000 threshold (add 23,500 at each bracket start).

q: How are part-time allowances taxed?
a: Taxed at a flat 30% on gross part-time earnings; employees may file a return of total emoluments to claim any overpaid tax.

q: What are employer obligations for PAYE?
a: Withhold correct tax when paying liable employees; remit withheld tax by the 15th of the following month; provide accountability per employee monthly; keep records for at least 5 years for URA inspection.

q: What are employee obligations and rights?
a: If earning from multiple sources, file an annual return declaring all income and taxes paid (PAYE/withholding/provisional). If only one employment fully taxed, no return required. Employees can claim refunds for overpaid tax and are entitled to accountability for taxes deducted and remitted.

q: What is Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI)?
a: Systematic yearly exchange of bulk non-resident financial account information between source and residence countries to enhance tax transparency and compliance.

q: Legal basis for AEOI in Uganda
a: Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (Implementation) Act 2023, domestication of the MAAC, the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement (MCAA), and the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) set reporting and due-diligence obligations.

q: Why Automatic Exchange of Information?
a: Globalisation enables offshore evasion; AEOI increases transparency to detect and deter non-compliance and improve compliance.

q: Benefits of AEOI
a: Timely data on evasion risks; detects previously unknown non-compliance; deters evasion; raises revenue; supports fairness in taxation.

q: What financial institutions are covered?
a: Custodial institutions; depository institutions; investment entities; specified insurance companies.

q: What accounts are covered by AEOI?
a: Custodial accounts; depository accounts; equity or debt interests in investment entities; cash value insurance and annuity contracts.

q: What types of information can be exchanged?
a: Identification (name, address, jurisdiction of residence, TIN, DOB), account number and reporting FI; financial data such as year-end balance/closure, gross interest/dividends/other income, gross proceeds (custodial), gross interest (deposits), cash value or surrender value (insurance), and gross payments for other accounts.

q: How is confidentiality and security guaranteed?
a: Secure point-to-point exchange between FIs and URA; URA to OECD via the Common Transmission System (CTS); stringent confidentiality and data safeguards.

q: When must reporting financial institutions report?
a: Annually for accounts held by non-residents/reportable accounts for the year ending 31 December; submit to URA by 31 May of the following year.

q: What if no reportable accounts are found?
a: File a Nil return after applying due diligence for the calendar year.

q: What are pre-existing vs new accounts for due diligence?
a: Pre-existing account: maintained on or before 31 Dec 2023. New account: opened on/after 1 Jan 2024. Due-diligence rules vary by category.

q: Consequences for failing to fulfil reporting obligations
a: Penalties under Section 8 of the Act: UGX 5,000,000 per day for failure to file; UGX 10,000,000 plus UGX 400,000 per day for failing to maintain due-diligence records; up to UGX 50,000,000 and/or up to 10 years imprisonment for false or misleading returns/self-certifications or omissions.

q: How will AEOI information be protected?
a: Implementation under ISO 27001-style controls: secure networks, monitoring, backups, controlled access, high data-safeguard standards; information shared only with jurisdictions that have AEOI agreements and equivalent security.

q: Who are reportable persons for AEOI?
a: Non-resident individuals or entities (tax resident outside Uganda) with financial accounts in Uganda; FIs collect and send data to URA, which transmits to the relevant tax jurisdictions.

q: How will individuals and entities be affected?
a: FIs must report accounts of reportable persons; Ugandan-only tax residents are not reported externally. Due diligence and self-certification may be requested to confirm residency.

q: What is a self-certification?
a: A declaration of an account holder’s tax residence; knowingly false or misleading self-certifications can attract fines up to UGX 50,000,000 and/or up to 10 years imprisonment.

q: Why am I asked to provide tax residency in the self-certification?
a: Due diligence requirements under the Act compel FIs to identify tax residency of account holders/controlling persons for AEOI reporting.

q: Do Ugandan-only tax residents need to provide self-certification for new and pre-existing accounts?
a: New accounts: self-certification required. Pre-existing accounts: FIs conduct due diligence and may request self-certification if needed or may apply new-account procedures to old accounts.

q: What if my tax residency changes?
a: Notify the FI of changes affecting tax residency and provide an updated self-certification, generally within 30 days of the change.

q: How do I know if I am tax resident in another jurisdiction?
a: Tax residence is defined by each jurisdiction’s laws and can be multiple; paying a tax abroad does not alone create residency. Consult guidance or professional advice; see OECD CRS tax residency resources.

q: I am only tax resident in Uganda. Will my information be reported abroad?
a: No. If you are not tax resident outside Uganda, your account information should not be reported to other jurisdictions under AEOI.

q: Joint account where one holder is tax resident abroad; will both be reported?
a: The joint account is reported (in full, no apportionment) for the holder who is tax resident in the partner jurisdiction; the spouse who is not tax resident abroad is not reported.

q: Ugandan resident with property abroad—will the account be reported?
a: Ownership of foreign property alone does not create tax residency; if not tax resident of that country, the Ugandan account is not reported to that jurisdiction.

q: Account held for benefit of spouse not tax resident of Country C—will it be exchanged?
a: No. The spouse is the account holder/beneficiary and is not tax resident of Country C, so the account is not exchanged to Country C.

q: Will URA specify who is a tax resident of each foreign jurisdiction?
a: No. Each jurisdiction defines its own tax residence. FIs collect self-certifications for new accounts and perform due diligence on pre-existing accounts; self-certification may be requested if status is unclear.

q: Definition of Uganda tax resident for AEOI purposes
a: Resident if: individual has a permanent home in Uganda, or spends ≥183 days in 12 months, or averages >122 days over current and two prior years, or is a government employee posted abroad; company incorporated/managed/major operations in Uganda; trust established/managed or with resident trustee; partnership with any resident partner.

q: Why Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI)?
a: Globalisation enables offshore investment and tax evasion; AEOI improves transparency and tax compliance by automatically sharing financial account data on non-residents.

q: What types of financial institutions are covered by AEOI?
a: Custodial institutions; Depository institutions; Investment entities; Specified insurance companies.

q: What types of accounts are covered by AEOI?
a: Custodial accounts; Depository accounts; Equity or debt interests in investment entities; Cash value insurance contracts and annuity contracts.

q: How is confidentiality and security of exchanges guaranteed?
a: Uganda must maintain high confidentiality and data safeguards; exchanges use secure point-to-point communications. URA exchanges with the OECD via the Common Transmission System (CTS).

q: When must reporting financial institutions submit information to URA?
a: Annually for the calendar year ending 31 December, due by 31 May of the following year.

q: What if no reportable accounts are found after due diligence?
a: The reporting financial institution must file a Nil return.

q: Pre-existing and new account dates for due diligence
a: Pre-existing accounts are those maintained as of 31 December 2023. New accounts are those opened on or after 1 January 2024. Due-diligence procedures differ between the two categories.

q: Consequences of failing to fulfill reporting obligations
a: Under the Act, penalties include: UGX 5,000,000 per day for failure to file returns; UGX 10,000,000 plus UGX 400,000 per day for failure to maintain due-diligence records; up to UGX 50,000,000 and/or up to 10 years’ imprisonment for false or misleading statements or omissions related to AEOI returns or self-certifications.

q: Who are the reportable persons for AEOI?
a: Financial institutions in Uganda identify accounts of non-resident individuals or entities (tax-resident outside Uganda), report them to URA, and URA transmits to the relevant tax jurisdiction.

q: How are individuals and entities affected by AEOI?
a: Only reportable (non-Uganda-resident) persons are reported. Purely Uganda-resident taxpayers are not reported. FIs must collect required information via due diligence and self-certifications.

q: Why must I provide tax residency in the self-certification?
a: Due-diligence rules in the Act require FIs to identify the tax residency of account holders and controlling persons for AEOI reporting.

q: Do Ugandan-only tax residents need to self-certify?
a: Yes. For new accounts, self-certification is required. For pre-existing accounts, FIs conduct due diligence and may request self-certification if needed.

q: How do I know if I am a tax resident of another jurisdiction?
a: Tax residence is determined by each jurisdiction’s domestic law; a person may have multiple tax residences. Paying some taxes abroad does not by itself create tax residence. Refer to the OECD CRS tax-residency portal or seek professional advice if unsure.

q: Will Ugandan-only residents be reported abroad?
a: If you are not tax-resident outside Uganda, your accounts should not be reported by FIs to URA for transmission to other jurisdictions.

q: Joint account where one holder is tax-resident abroad
a: If one holder is tax-resident in Country A, the full joint account is reported to Country A under AEOI. The co-holder not tax-resident abroad is not reported.

q: Ugandan resident owning property abroad
a: Owning property or paying related taxes abroad does not alone make you tax-resident there; if you are not tax-resident in that country, your Ugandan account is not reported to it.

q: Account held for non-resident spouse but spouse is account holder
a: Only the beneficiary/account holder’s tax residence matters. If the spouse (account holder) is not tax-resident in Country C, the account is not exchanged to Country C.

q: Will URA specify overseas tax residents?
a: No. Each jurisdiction defines its own tax residence. FIs obtain self-certifications for new accounts and perform due diligence on pre-existing accounts; they may seek self-certification if in doubt.

q: Is exempt income the same as a tax deduction?
a: No. A tax deduction reduces taxable income; exempt income is excluded from taxable income altogether.

q: What allowances or incomes are exempt from income tax?
a: Examples include: income of listed First Schedule institutions; income of persons with Diplomatic Privilege Act immunities; official income of foreign public servants paid from and taxed in their country; allowances paid abroad to Ugandan foreign mission staff; all income of local authorities; income of URA-certified exempt organisations except unrelated business/property income; bona fide education grants; court-ordered alimony/allowance; gifts/bequests/inheritance not forming business/employment/property income; capital gains outside business (except on private company shares or commercial buildings); technical assistance employment income (non-resident or resident solely for that work, with ministerial concurrence); foreign-source income of short-term residents/foreign public servants/technical assistance staff and immediate family; pensions; lump-sum from resident retirement fund to member/dependent; life insurance proceeds; official employment income of UPDF/UPF/ESO/ISO/Prisons (non-civilian); MP employment income except salary; DPP prosecutors’ employment income; income of GoU and other governments; Bank of Uganda income; collective investment scheme income distributed to participants; EADB employee emoluments; investor compensation fund income; deposit protection fund income; income of aircraft operators in domestic/international traffic; income of exporters of finished consumer and capital goods (subject to conditions); sports awards for winning/participating; SACCO income; income from letting/leasing in industrial park/free zone (conditions); income of operators in industrial park/free zone (conditions); interest on infrastructure bonds; dividends of companies created via stock exchange listing.

q: What is an export of goods?
a: Taking goods/services from Uganda to a foreign country. Intra-region transfers are within EAC; exports are to destinations outside EAC.

q: How are intra-region (EAC) cargo transfers processed?
a: Agent files declaration in importing country’s system; once released, it transmits to URA Asycuda; URA issues C2 (Cargo Movement Document); driver moves with C2; border officer performs exit and truck crosses to importing partner state.

q: How are exports outside the EAC processed?
a: Agent files declaration in exporting country system; once released, it transmits to KRA ICMS; at border URA exits consignment, KRA issues C2 and transits to port where export bond is discharged as cargo loads onto vessel.

q: What are the types of exports?
a: Permanent exports (remain/consumed abroad); temporary exports (to return after repair/exhibition etc.); re-exports (previously imported goods later exported—e.g., temporary imports, warehoused then exported, or home-consumed then exported).

q: Why export goods outside Uganda?
a: VAT/packing material refunds; customs taxes generally not charged on exports (except unprocessed hides/skins, fish, unprocessed tobacco); improves cash flow; note re-export income is taxable and must be declared.

q: Key exporter requirements
a: Have TIN; label goods “produced for export”; consult UEPB on labeling/buyers/pricing; appoint licensed customs agent; obtain export licence from UEPB; use licensed transporter; declare all transactional docs (invoice, packing list, etc.) in export entry.

q: Entry rules for export cargo
a: Enter all cargo with full particulars and evidence; export within 30 days of entry or extension by Commissioner; breaches liable to forfeiture (EACCMA).

q: Which exports can skip a SAD?
a: Bona fide passenger/crew baggage; goods for sale/delivery to passengers/crew; mail bags/postal articles in transit by post.

q: How is export value determined (FOB)?
a: Value at port/place of shipment plus charges to deliver on board. If cost unknown: use similar/identical exports at similar time; if still unknown, proper officer determines.

q: How are goods with export levy treated?
a: Duty stated on export entry; goods cannot be exported until duty paid or secured; discrepancies after exam are an offence and goods forfeitable; export duty not levied on goods grown/produced/manufactured in another Partner State (only subject to that State’s export rules).

q: Are exports taxed on income?
a: Income from re-exported goods is taxable and must be declared in returns to avoid penalties/interest.

q: When are export refunds/drawback available?
a: Refunds for packing materials and VAT on production inputs. For drawback: label goods for export; obtain export licence; compare export entry with import entry; no drawback on damaged/spoilt goods unless accidentally destroyed after loading and abandoned; not allowed on provisional entries—only fully cleared goods with invoice.

q: What are prohibited and restricted exports?
a: Prohibited: exports banned by law (EACCMA Third Schedule Part A, e.g., narcotics). Restricted: allowed only under conditions (Third Schedule Part B, e.g., scrap metals, charcoal, unprocessed fish, used batteries, timber). Goods on vessels <250 tons cannot include warehoused goods, duty-drawback goods, or transshipments.

q: What about goods in transit/transshipment?
a: Generally not affected by prohibited/restricted provisions; must be exported within time set by Commissioner.

q: How to handle temporary exports on re-import?
a: Obtain detailed examined export entry and re-importation certificate (Form P45) at export; on re-import, duty applies on value increase from repairs/additions/processing/other costs abroad. If repair was free under contractual obligation and Commissioner accepts, release without taxes (unless manufacturing defect accounted earlier).

q: What should I have in place before starting an export?
a: Register for a TIN, ensure the business is on URA’s system, and secure any sector permits for controlled goods (e.g., agriculture, minerals, wildlife products). Keep a valid sales contract, commercial invoice, and packing list ready.

q: Do I need a clearing agent to process exports?
a: You can self-clear, but most exporters appoint a licensed customs/clearing agent to lodge entries in ASYCUDA World and interface with the Uganda Electronic Single Window. Licensed agents are listed on the URA portal.

q: Which system is used to lodge export declarations?
a: Exports are declared electronically in ASYCUDA World (accessible through the Uganda Electronic Single Window). A Single Administrative Document (SAD) export entry is registered before goods leave.

q: Which documents are needed to lodge an export entry?
a: Typical documents include: commercial invoice, packing list, export contract or purchase order, transport document (BL/AWB/CMR), sector permits for controlled goods, certificate of origin if preferential treatment is sought, and any inspection or quality certificates required by the destination.

q: How are exports valued for customs purposes?
a: Exports are normally valued on a Free on Board (FOB) basis: the price paid for the goods plus costs up to loading on the international transport (local transport, handling, and insurance to the exit point).

q: Are export taxes payable in Uganda?
a: Most goods are not subject to export duty and are zero-rated for VAT; however, a few commodities attract export levies. Always check the current customs tariff and export-levy list for exceptions.

q: What are the key steps to clear goods for export at the border?
a: (1) Lodge the export SAD in ASYCUDA; (2) pay any applicable fees or levies; (3) present goods and documents for customs verification/scanning if required; (4) obtain release and exit note; (5) the carrier exits with sealed cargo.

q: How do I export goods from a bonded warehouse?
a: Request removal from bond for export, lodge the export SAD referencing the bonded goods, have the bond debited, present goods for customs verification/sealing, then obtain the exit note for movement out of Uganda.

q: Do I need a certificate of origin for exports?
a: It is optional unless the buyer or destination requires it for preferential duty. Obtain the appropriate certificate (e.g., EAC, COMESA, AGOA) from the authorized issuing body and attach it to the export entry.

q: How should samples or low-value promotional items be treated?
a: Declare them as exports in ASYCUDA with their true transaction value (even if sold at nominal value) and indicate the nature of the goods as samples. Customs may waive inspection but requires a proper declaration.

q: What should I do if my goods are consolidated with other exporters?
a: Provide your documents to the consolidator/clearing agent. Each shipper must have a house bill of lading/airwaybill showing the true owner and must lodge an export declaration for their cargo within the consolidated shipment.

q: Who can I contact for help with export procedures?
a: Reach URA through the toll-free lines 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000, WhatsApp 0772 140 000, or visit a customs office for guidance on export entries, permits, and system access.

q: What is a small business for tax purposes?
a: A business with annual sales above UGX 10m but not exceeding UGX 150m (per Income Tax Act Section 4(5) and Second Schedule).

q: Why do small businesses need financial management skills?
a: To plan, comply, and survive—most are sole proprietors with limited management skills; good financial skills improve continuity and growth.

q: What key financial management skills should a small business have?
a: Understand your market; create a financial plan and budget; know legal/regulatory requirements; keep business records; fulfill tax obligations; invest wisely.

q: How do I understand my market?
a: Research customers and preferences; track market trends; analyze competitors; estimate market size/growth to forecast income and expenses.

q: How do I create a financial plan?
a: Separate business vs personal finances; set goals; choose a reliable financial provider (SACCO/microfinance/bank); budget within income; save and invest; seek affordable financing with a repayment plan.

q: What legal/regulatory steps must I follow?
a: Register business name with URSB; obtain TIN via URA; get trading licence (KCCA/local authority); engage sector regulators (e.g., UNBS, NDA). For tax registration: individuals need National ID or two IDs; companies need certificate of incorporation, directors’ TINs, Form 7.

q: Why and how should I keep business records?
a: Accurate records show income/expenses and support sustainability. Ask for and issue receipts, record expenses, keep employee and tax records, maintain books for at least 5 years.

q: What are my tax obligations as a small business?
a: Register for taxes, file correct returns before due dates, pay on time, withhold PAYE where applicable, plan/estimate taxes early, seek URA help when unsure.

q: How do I pay small business income tax via URA?
a: On ura.go.ug: Make a payment → generate payment slip → choose Income Tax – Small Businesses → enter TIN/contact, assessment period, business details (name/activity/location/total sales), submit, then pay via bank or mobile money; URA does not handle cash.

q: How should I approach investing?
a: Set goals and an investment plan; diversify to manage risk; invest in businesses you understand; seek professional advice for large investments.

q: What gaming and pool betting activities are covered in Uganda?
a: National lottery, slot machines, bingo, virtual games, playing cards, casinos.

q: Who are the key players?
a: Licensed gaming/pool betting promoters (companies) and gamblers (individuals).

q: How do I register a gaming/pool betting business?
a: Register with URSB (company), URA (taxes), and local authority (trading licence); comply with National Lotteries and Gaming Regulatory Board requirements.

q: What do I need to register for taxes?
a: Individuals: National ID or two valid IDs (passport, driving permit, voter’s card, work permit, etc.), certificate of registration if in business, partnership deed if applicable. Non-individuals: Form 20 and certificate of incorporation.

q: How do I register for taxes online?
a: Use the URA portal (ura.go.ug); choose individual or non-individual registration as applicable.

q: What are my taxpayer rights and obligations?
a: See URA guidance; know your rights and obligations as a taxpayer (links provided by URA).

q: What business records must I keep?
a: Keep records for at least five years: income statement, weekly stake records, payouts and winner IDs, import schedules, bank statements, receipts/invoices, debtors/creditors records.

q: What taxes apply to gaming/pool betting promoters?
a: Gaming tax: (Total stakes − payouts) × 30% (promoter pays). Betting tax: (Total stakes − payouts) × 20% (promoter pays); payouts attract 15% withholding as final tax withheld from winners. PAYE: register and withhold for employees earning > UGX 235,000/month. WHT: promoters register and withhold on winnings as final tax.

q: How do I file returns?
a: Submit weekly returns by Wednesday of the following week for gaming/pool betting.

q: How do I pay URA taxes?
a: After filing, pay via banks, mobile money, cards (Mastercard/VISA), EFT/RTGS, USSD *285#, etc. Payment due date matches return due date; late payment attracts 2% weekly interest on outstanding tax.

q: What must I have when importing via groupage (shared containers)?
a: Obtain a Tax Identification Number (TIN) to declare and pay taxes for your goods.

q: What checklist should I follow for groupage imports?
a: Use only registered cargo consolidators; know your shipper and cargo contents; keep invoices/receipts and records; request the customs entry number; get a packing list; know the tax due; be present for customs verification.

q: Key security tip for groupage imports?
a: Do not share your TIN or password to prevent unauthorised clearance in your name.

q: Benefits of clearing with your own TIN?
a: Faster processing; ability to claim WHT/VAT refunds; direct relationship with URA; access to pre-import guidance/support; full visibility and control of clearance.

q: Step-by-step: how do I clear groupage cargo using my TIN?
a: 1) Shipment: shipping line issues master bill; consolidator splits to house bills; importer gets their house bill. 2) Port clearance (Mombasa/Dar): consolidator’s agent files WT8 to URA; once approved, goods move in transit to a bonded warehouse in Uganda. 3) Arrival/verification: warehouse keeper and URA receive shipment; each importer appoints an agent for their house bill; URA verifies shipment with importers/agents. 4) Transfer of ownership: consolidator requests transfer in ASYCUDA to each importer’s TIN with house bill; URA approves and updates ownership. 5) Tax payment: importer’s agent files IM4 home-use declaration and pays due taxes; URA verifies payment. 6) Release: URA physically releases goods to the importer.

q: Who is eligible for Instant TIN?
a: Only individuals registered with NIRA who have a valid National Identification Number (NIN).

q: Do I need URA staff approval for an instant TIN?
a: No. The online form issues a TIN automatically; there is no manual verification or approval in this flow.

q: What if I do not have a NIN?
a: You cannot use Instant TIN. Apply through the standard Individual TIN or Non-Individual TIN registration options instead.

q: What information is required to apply?
a: Your NIN, full name (as on the national ID), title, marital status, source of income, address, email, and mobile number.

q: How do I apply for an instant TIN?
a: Go to ura.go.ug → click Get a TIN → choose Instant TIN → select Individual → enter NIN and personal details → confirm you are not a robot → submit.

q: How long does it take to get the TIN?
a: About five minutes after submitting the instant TIN form.

q: How will I receive my TIN?
a: The TIN is sent to the mobile phone number and email address provided in the form.

q: Is there a fee for Instant TIN?
a: No, applying for an instant TIN is free on the URA portal.

q: What should I do if the TIN is not delivered?
a: Verify the phone/email you entered, check spam/SMS inbox, and retry. If still missing, contact URA support for assistance.

q: Who can I contact for help?
a: Call URA toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000 or WhatsApp 0772 140 000 for instant TIN support.

q: What is hosted under Laws, Acts and Regulations?
a: A catalog of URA-related laws, regulations, reports, and manuals (e.g., tax laws, EAC customs acts, duty remission rules, VAT and excise amendments, AML regulations, CET schedules).

q: How do I download a law or act?
a: Open the Laws, Acts and Regulations page, pick the title you need, and click the associated Download link in its row to fetch the file.

q: Can I sort or filter the list?
a: Yes. Use the Order By dropdown (Publish Date, Title, Update Date, Downloads, Views) and choose Ascending/Descending, then Apply Filter to reorder the list.

q: Do I need to log in to download files?
a: No login is required to download the listed laws and acts; the links are public.

q: What file formats should I expect?
a: Items are typically provided as PDFs or document attachments; each row shows the file count, and the Download link retrieves the document.

q: Are the Acts up to date?
a: The page includes recent amendments (e.g., VAT, Excise, Lotteries and Gaming, Traffic and Road Safety 2023, AML Regulations 2023). Always confirm the publication or update date in the document and cross-check with the latest Gazette if needed.

q: Where can I find regional customs references?
a: The listing includes the East African Community Customs Management Act, Rules of Origin, Duty Remission Regulations, and the Common External Tariff schedule.

q: Who can I contact if a link is broken?
a: Reach URA support via toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000, WhatsApp 0772 140 000, or visit a URA office for assistance with access to legal documents.

q: What is a PRN and why do I need it?
a: A Payment Registration Number (PRN) uniquely identifies your tax payment. You must quote it when paying at the bank, via mobile money, or online card channels so the payment is matched to your tax account.

q: How do I generate a PRN?
a: On the URA portal, go to Make a Payment → Generate a Payment Slip, select the tax type/period, confirm amounts, and submit to obtain the PRN (and slip) to present to your payment channel.

q: Where can I pay after getting a PRN?
a: Use partnered banks, mobile money (by quoting the PRN), or online card payments (Visa/Mastercard) available from the Make a Payment section.

q: Can I pay by Visa or MasterCard online?
a: Yes. Choose Pay with VISA or Master Card under Make a Payment, enter the PRN and follow the card payment flow.

q: What if my PRN expired?
a: Use Reactivate Expired PRN on the Make a Payment page to refresh the reference before paying.

q: How do I confirm the payment posted?
a: Use View Payment Status on the URA portal with your PRN to see if the payment was received.

q: Can I reprint a payment slip?
a: Yes. Select Print a Payment Slip in the Make a Payment menu and enter the PRN to reprint.

q: Can I verify an advance income tax payment?
a: Yes. Use Verify Advance Income Tax Payment in the Make a Payment section and supply the PRN/payment details.

q: Is there a way to pay park user fees or hospital fees?
a: Yes. The Make a Payment page includes dedicated options to generate PRNs for park user fees and to pay for hospital fees.

q: Who can help if a payment fails or is not reflected?
a: Contact URA support via toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000 or WhatsApp 0772 140 000 with your PRN and payment receipt for assistance.

q: What is passenger baggage?
a: Accompanied or unaccompanied luggage of a returning resident or a non‑resident arriving from outside Uganda; must be accompanied by the owner or authorized person.

q: What are personal effects?
a: Articles (new or used) a passenger may need for personal or household use during/after the journey, excluding goods for commercial purposes and subject to limits set by the Commissioner.

q: General conditions for baggage exemptions
a: Goods must belong to the passenger, be for personal/household use, be accompanied, and in quantities/kinds the customs officer allows under Part B of the 5th Schedule to EACCMA (with stated restrictions).

q: Which goods are NOT exempt as passenger baggage/personal effects?
a: Alcoholic beverages, perfumes, spirits, tobacco products (except duty‑free allowances); fabrics in piece; trade goods or goods for sale/disposal; unprocessed foods, agricultural items, live pets (need relevant ministry clearance); all medicaments need NDA/ministry clearance.

q: Duty-free allowances (18+ only)
a: Spirits ≤1L or wine ≤2L; perfume/toilet water ≤500ml (max 250ml perfume); tobacco products ≤250g total. Excess quantities attract tax regardless of intended use.

q: Bona fide changing residence – what is exempt?
a: On first arrival/return when changing residence into a Partner State: wearing apparel; personal/household effects previously used; one motor vehicle (not buses/minibuses >13 seats or load trucks >2 tons) owned/used outside a Partner State for ≥12 months (voyage time excluded).

q: Temporary visit (≤3 months) – what can be exempt?
a: Non‑consumable goods for personal use to be taken out on departure; consumables and non‑alcoholic beverages in reasonable quantities; applies also to recalled staff of international organizations headquartered in a Partner State.

q: Returning travellers – what is exempt?
a: Wearing apparel and personal/household effects in prior use; plus goods for personal use valued up to USD 2,000 as accompanied baggage, declared, after being outside Uganda >24 hours.

q: How are passengers cleared (red/green channels)?
a: At gazetted points (airports, seaports, land borders). Green: nothing to declare within allowances. Red: goods to declare (dutiable/restricted). Present receipts/invoices; misdeclaration is an offence under EACCMA (up to 3 years imprisonment or fine ≤USD 10,000).

q: Key procedural notes for baggage clearance (PB4 small consignments)
a: Goods removed must be registered and issued a deposit note; PB4 reference = deposit note; only release to holder of valid deposit note; capture only verified goods; goods by air/bus must clear within 12 hours; PB4 applies where value ≤USD 2,000.

q: Summary of PB4 step flow
a: Receive goods and issue deposit slip; capture PB4 with verification and documents (ID, invoices, receipts, manifest, origin cert if any); assess taxes using indicative values; client pays; officer confirms payment, releases and supervises loading/hand‑over; generate exit note; update register with entry, taxes, PRN, exit.

q: What new income tax holiday was introduced?
a: Ugandan-owned businesses registered after 1 July 2025 get a three-year income tax exemption if initial capital is ≤ UGX 500m, the owner/associate has not benefited before, and they file returns including business info as prescribed.

q: How long is Bujagali hydropower income tax relief extended?
a: Exempt until 30 June 2026 to keep power costs lower and investor confidence high.

q: How was corporate reorganisation relief expanded?
a: Roll-over relief now covers transfers to another person (not an individual) controlled by the transferor/shareholders where transferee stock is distributed.

q: What change was made to digital service tax?
a: No DST applies where a non-resident provides digital services to an associate in Uganda (related-party transactions excluded).

q: Which institution was added to the listed institutions?
a: International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

q: What VAT changes affect public international bodies?
a: Schedule 2 adds UN-related and specialised agencies (including correcting IAEA name) to allow VAT refund relief.

q: Which supplies gained VAT exemption?
a: Deep cycle batteries, solar lanterns and raw materials for them; wet processing/garmenting inputs (cotton lint, fibres, dyes, machinery parts, accessories); biomass pellets. Terminology shifts from “composite lanterns” to “solar lanterns.”

q: Which VAT exemption was repealed?
a: Exemption for billets for further value addition was removed to spur local billet production.

q: What VAT zero-rating change was made?
a: Supply of aircraft is zero-rated to reduce acquisition costs and encourage fleet investment.

q: How was excise duty refunds improved?
a: Businesses can apply to offset excise paid on damaged/expired/obsolete goods against other tax liabilities (or other taxes if elected) upon proof.

q: What excise rate adjustments were made?
a: Tobacco: soft cap sticks UGX 65k/1000 (local) and UGX 150k/1000 (imported); hinge lid UGX 90k/1000 (local) and UGX 200k/1000 (imported). Beer with ≥75% local raw material: 30% or UGX 900/L (higher). Fruit/veg juice (except ≥50% local pulp) 10% or UGX 250/L (higher). Plastics: sacks/bags HS 3923.21/3923.29 at 2.5% or USD 70/ton (higher) with exclusions (vacuum food bags, tea/coffee sacks, sanitary pad bags).

q: What stamp duty relief was introduced?
a: Nil duty for agreements/memoranda, mortgage deeds, and crop mortgages to lower financing costs.

q: What new TIN/ID requirements apply?
a: For tax purposes use NIN for individuals, URSB registration number for non-individuals, or a foreign TIN from a treaty partner. Authorities must require these before issuing licenses or registering stamp-duty instruments.

q: What waiver is available for outstanding taxes?
a: Interest and penalties outstanding as of 30 June 2024 are waived pro-rata if part of the principal is paid by 30 June 2026.

q: What are new penalties around EFRIS and gaming?
a: EFRIS: penal tax of double the tax due on the goods/services. Gaming/betting: operators must use the centralised payments gateway; non-use triggers penal tax of double the gaming/WHT due or 5,500 currency points, whichever is higher.

q: What compliance rule was added for tax-exempt entities?
a: Exempt taxpayers must continuously meet exemption conditions or become personally liable for the tax during non-compliant periods.

q: Which customs duty remissions were granted for FY 2025/26?
a: One-year remissions to 0%/lower rates on: scaffolding pipes and cup-lock systems; melamine resins for kitchenware; stainless steel flat-rolled inputs for pipes; paper/paperboard for beer/cigarette labels; lacquers/varnish for metallic labels; printing inks (UV/metallic) for labels; certain cartons/PVC sheets for pharma packaging; plus reduced rates to support local manufacturing.

q: How do I make a payment on the URA portal?
a: Steps: 1) Go to ura.go.ug and click Make a payment. 2) Under Generate a payment slip choose “Click here to register a payment.” 3) Enter taxpayer details (TIN, name, district), select tax period and basis of payment. 4) Choose the correct tax head and load periods. 5) Add the period, fill the amount. 6) Complete the payment method captcha, click Accept and Register. 7) A payment registration slip is generated; note the PRN and pay via bank/mobile money or other modes.

q: How do I apply for a Learners/Provisional Driving Permit?
a: Pay NTR via URA portal (Payment registration → NTR head → fill mandatory fields → accept & register → pay bank). Download permit forms (TR VII) from Domestic taxes > manual forms, attach medical form, submit to Face Technology. Applicant must be 18+; starter classes include A, B, H. Provisional permit valid 3 months and renewable.

q: How do I apply for a Full Permit?
a: Register and pay NTR via URA portal (payment registration); download TR VII permit form; fill form with required attachments; present stamped bank slip and form to Face Technology for processing.

q: How do I apply for Driving Permit Exchange (foreign permit)?
a: Register and pay NTR via URA portal (payment registration). Download TR VII form, fill, attach required docs (medical form, work permit/defendant’s pass/ID per status, translation if needed, etc.), submit with stamped payment slip to Face Technology.

q: How do I renew my permit?
a: Register and pay NTR via URA portal (payment registration). Download Form XII (permit renewal) under permit forms, fill it, attach required docs, submit with stamped bank slip to Face Technology.

q: How do I add a class to my permit (extension)?
a: Register and pay NTR via URA portal (payment registration). Download TR VII form, fill for extension of classes, attach required docs incl. medical form, submit with stamped payment slip to Face Technology.

q: How do I apply for a duplicate permit?
a: Register and pay NTR via URA portal (payment registration). Download TR VII form, fill for duplicate, attach required docs (medical form). For lost permits add police statement and newspaper advert; for change of particulars add affidavit/gazette; pay duplicate fees; submit to Face Technology with stamped bank slip.

q: How do I validate motor vehicle details (new registration book)?
a: Login to ura.go.ug with TIN/password → e-services → Motor vehicle registration → Add vehicle details → fill required pages and submit. Print e-acknowledgment; wait for approval notice via email/portal, then obtain new logbook.

q: How do I apply for duplicate registration books/number plates?
a: Must have validated vehicle/new logbook. Login with TIN → e-services → Motor Vehicle Registration → Applications → new form → purpose duplicate. Fill pages, attach docs, register payment, print acknowledgment and payment slip, pay at bank, submit to Licensing office for processing.

q: How do I apply for change of ownership (vehicle transfer)?
a: Requires new logbook in your names. Login → e-services → Motor Vehicle registration → Applications → new form → purpose Change of ownership. Fill mandatory fields, enter buyer’s TIN and reason, attach docs, register payment, print receipt/form/payment slip, pay bank, submit to Licensing office with attachments.

q: How do I re-register a motor vehicle (change plate category)?
a: Requires new logbook. Login → e-services → Motor Vehicle registration → Applications → new form → purpose Re-Registration; choose new plate category; attach docs; register payment; print acknowledgment/form/payment slip; pay bank; submit to Licensing office with attachments.

q: How do I apply for alteration of particulars on a motor vehicle?
a: Requires new logbook. Login → e-services → Motor Vehicle registration → Applications → new form → purpose Alteration; select fields to alter; edit vehicle details; attach docs; register payment; print acknowledgment/form/payment slip; pay bank; submit to Licensing office.

q: How do I de-register a motor vehicle?
a: Requires new logbook. Login → e-services → Motor Vehicle registration → Applications → new form → purpose De-Registration; specify reason; attach docs; register payment; print acknowledgment/form/payment slip; pay bank; submit to Licensing office with attachments.

q: How do I transfer a vehicle if I can’t trace the owner (absentee transferor)?
a: Prepare affidavit with stamp duty, newspaper public notice, court order instructing transfer, ID copies, original logbook and transfer forms; present vehicle for inspection; fees assessed; submit application with attachments (include 14-day newspaper advert) for approval.

q: How do I search and certify motor vehicle details?
a: Only for vehicles with new logbooks. On ura.go.ug → e-services → motor vehicle → search & certification; enter applicant TIN (or No), vehicle number, select application type, register payment, print payment slip, pay bank. After payment use reference/search code to view details online; certification copies issued by Licensing office if paid for certification.

q: How do I endorse third-party interest (caveat) on a motor vehicle?
a: For vehicles with new logbooks. Interested party writes to licensing office, declares instrument, pays stamp duty; documents acknowledged and endorsement fee (UGX 50,000) assessed; pay bank and present evidence; upon confirmation, registration book issued with third-party endorsement.

q: How do I renew a dealer’s plate license?
a: Login with TIN → e-services → Motor Vehicle registration → Dealer’s License applications; fill mandatory fields, attach docs, register payment (select head/subhead), choose bank/mode, submit; print acknowledgment/form/payment slip; pay bank; submit to Licensing office with attachments.

q: How do I renew an OTV license?
a: Login with TIN → e-services → Motor Vehicle registration → Owner’s Transport Vehicle applications; fill mandatory fields, attach docs, register payment (select head/subhead), choose bank/mode, submit; print acknowledgment/form/payment slip; pay bank; submit to Licensing office with attachments.

q: How do I get or renew PMO and PSV license?
a: Handled at Transport Licensing Board. URA role: register payment online. On ura.go.ug → e-services → Payment registration → Tax head Other NTR → Details of other NTR: Ministry of Works and Transport → select PSV/PMO and category → complete slip, accept & register, print and pay bank; take payment evidence to Transport Licensing Board for processing.

q: What is a return filing?
a: A return of income is a declaration to URA of income (or loss) for a period (e.g., PAYE, income tax, VAT, LED, WHT, GPBT, etc.).

q: Who is eligible to file a return?
a: Anyone with chargeable income (except resident individuals below threshold); resident companies file on global income; partnerships file returns.

q: Who is not required to file a return?
a: Non-residents whose Uganda-sourced income is fully subject to final WHT; resident individuals with only single-employer PAYE income; resident individuals below chargeable-income threshold.

q: What are the due dates for filing returns?
a: Provisional (individual): 3 months after start of year; Provisional (non-individual): 6 months after start; VAT/PAYE/WHT/LED (services): 15th of following month; LED (goods): 21st; GPBT: weekly.

q: What is the difference between provisional and final return?
a: Provisional: estimated income/tax for the current/next period. Final: actual income/tax for the completed period.

q: How do I file a return?
a: Login ura.go.ug with TIN/password → e-services → e-returns → select return type and download template; enable macros, fill without renaming or copy/paste; validate to generate upload file; back to e-returns upload file with return period and captcha; submit; e-acknowledgment is issued (also emailed/portal).

q: How do I amend an already filed return?
a: Login → e-services → e-returns → amendments → select return type; enter period, download original return (encrypted), open and set status to amended with original ref/date; change details, validate to create upload file; upload via amendment section and submit; acknowledgment is issued.

q: How do I print a submitted return or view history?
a: Login → e-services → e-returns → View History; choose period and form, click show; open reference number (blue link) to print forms and receipt.

q: How do I deal with an Error code on return upload"?"
a: Do not rename templates or copy/cut/paste values. Keep the system-provided filename and adhere to defined formats; renaming or pasting breaks security and causes upload errors.

q: Are religious institutions taxable?
a: Core religious receipts (offertories, tithes, fundraising) are exempt from income tax, but business activities, taxable supplies, and imports/exports are taxable and must comply.

q: When is a religious institution exempt?
a: If its income/assets do not confer private benefit, and it holds an exemption letter from the URA Commissioner General confirming not-for-profit religious purpose.

q: Who governs religious groups nationally?
a: The Inter-Religious Council of Uganda (affiliated to WCRP/ACRL) brings major denominations together.

q: How do religious-owned businesses get a TIN (non-individual)?
a: On ura.go.ug: Get a TIN → TIN Registration – Non-Individual → download Excel template, fill mandatory fields, validate, save upload, upload and submit, then print acknowledgement and form; submit signed form, terms, and IDs to URA.

q: How do individuals (e.g., clergy) get an instant TIN?
a: On ura.go.ug: Get a TIN → Instant TIN Application → apply as Individual with NIN, source of income, address; submit to receive instant TIN and provisional certificate.

q: What are key taxpayer rights?
a: Fair treatment, privacy/confidentiality, to be informed, to challenge/appeal and seek refunds, representation, and timely service.

q: What are key taxpayer obligations?
a: Register, file accurate/timely returns, keep records 5+ years, pay taxes, avoid evasion, quote TIN in dealings, update details, be respectful, and use authorized staff/channels.

q: What records should be kept?
a: Income/receipts, payroll, contracts, bank statements, utility bills, stock records, asset registers, invoices/receipts, debtors/creditors—retain at least 5 years.

q: Which taxes can apply to religious institutions?
a: Income tax on business income (30% companies; individual rates); rental tax on let property (12% individuals; 30% companies); PAYE on staff pay above UGX 235,000; WHT (e.g., 6% on goods/services to designated agents; 10–15% on specific payments); presumptive tax if turnover 10m–150m and not in excluded professions.

q: What is the presumptive tax scale?
When must a religious entity register for VAT?
a: If making taxable supplies and turnover exceeds UGX 37.5m in any 3 consecutive months (UGX 150m annual); must register and use EFRIS, file/pay monthly.

q: How are dividends handled?
a: Resident companies must withhold 15% on dividends to resident shareholders unless exempt (e.g., listed company 10% rate applies).

q: What are key return due dates?
a: Provisional income tax: individuals by last day of 3rd month; companies by last day of 6th month of year. Final income tax: within 6 months after year end. Monthly: WHT/PAYE/VAT/excise/gaming by 15th of following month.

q: How do institutions pay taxes?
a: After filing, pay via banks, mobile money, EFT/RTGS, VISA/Mastercard, USSD *285#, etc.

q: What is rental income?
a: Total money earned from renting immovable property (land and/or buildings) in Uganda for a year of income, net of any expenditure incurred on that property.

q: What is rental income tax?
a: Tax on the total income earned from leasing immovable property in Uganda, after deducting expenditure incurred on that property.

q: Who pays rental income tax?
a: The person earning the rental income—the landlord or landlady (property owner) who lets out the property.

q: What counts as rented property?
a: Houses for rent, commercial buildings for rent, and land leased to telecom companies or similar users.

q: Who can be a landlord/landlady?
a: Any person letting out immovable property: individuals, companies, corporate bodies, government entities, institutions, or listed institutions.

q: Who is a tenant?
a: Anyone occupying another person’s property in exchange for payment.

q: How is rental income treated under tax law?
a: Rental income is governed by Section 5 of the Income Tax Act and is taxed separately from other income sources.

q: What is smuggling?
a: Importing/exporting or moving goods with intent to defraud customs, evade taxes, or bypass prohibitions/restrictions; it is illegal and often driven by greed, ignorance, or weak nationalism.

q: What are common forms of smuggling?
a: Outright border evasion (lake, road, rail, bush), under-declaration of quantities, undervaluation, misclassification to lower duty, falsified documents, misdeclared origin (e.g., false COMESA), and diverting transit/re-export goods into Uganda.

q: Why do some goods face restrictions or prohibitions?
a: To protect the economy (local industries/markets), safeguard health and environment, and ensure security (e.g., firearms controls).

q: What is the difference between restricted and prohibited goods?
a: Restricted: allowed only under set conditions/regulations. Prohibited: not allowed under customs or other Partner State laws.

q: What are the effects of smuggling?
a: Revenue loss; price distortions and unfair competition; harm to local industries and jobs; health risks from substandard goods; increased insecurity (e.g., smuggled firearms).

q: Is smuggling an offence?
a: Yes. It is an offence under the East African Community Customs Management Act (EACCMA).

q: How can I report smuggling?
a: Report to URA Regional Managers or Assistant Commissioner Enforcement; if your tip leads to tax recovery, Section 242 EACCMA allows a reward.

q: What is stamp duty?
a: A non-tax revenue on instruments listed in Schedule 2 of the Stamp Duty Act (Cap. 339), payable on documents executed or received in Uganda that create, transfer, limit, extend, extinguish, or record rights or liabilities.

q: Who pays stamp duty?
a: The person drawing/making/executing (signing) the instrument.

q: How is compliance enforced for informal parties?
a: Public offices that must act on instruments (e.g., land registrars, URSB) require proof of paid stamp duty before processing; purely private in-house documents are harder to police.

q: Who must have stamp duty?
a: Anyone executing or receiving a Schedule 2 instrument in Uganda—per Section 3 of the Act, the drawer/maker is liable.

q: Do you register for stamp duty?
a: No separate registration; you simply declare and pay when an applicable instrument is executed/received.

q: When is stamp duty due?
a: Within 45 days of executing an instrument in Uganda, or within 30 days of receiving one executed abroad (per Sections 13 and 14).

q: Which transactions are exempt?
a: Instruments executed by Government and public international institutions in the Second Schedule of the VAT and Income Tax Acts, plus any instruments specifically exempted by the Minister of Finance.

q: Does non-payment void the document?
a: No, but the instrument is inadmissible as evidence in commercial courts until duty is paid.

q: Is there a minimum threshold?
a: No; stamp duty applies to every dutiable instrument regardless of value.

q: What are penalties for non-payment?
a: Conviction can lead to a UGX 2,000,000 fine or up to 6 months’ imprisonment, or both, for executing an instrument without paying proper duty.

q: What is withholding tax exemption?
a: It is approval to stop deducting/withholding income tax at source for a qualifying taxpayer or transaction as allowed by URA.

q: Who can apply for withholding tax exemption?
a: Taxpayers with a valid TIN who meet exemption conditions (e.g., listed in WHT exemption categories) can apply through their URA portal account.

q: How do I apply for a WHT exemption?
a: Log in to the URA web portal with your TIN and password → e-Services → e-Registration → Tax Exemption Application → complete the form and submit.

q: Which credentials do I need to apply?
a: Your active TIN credentials (username/password) to access the URA portal and file the e-Registration Tax Exemption Application.

q: How do I download my exemption certificate?
a: Log in to the URA portal → e-Services → Taxpayer Profile → choose Print Tax/Exemption Certificate (PDF download).

q: Where do I track my exemption application status?
a: Use Track Application Status on the URA portal after submitting the exemption application.

q: What if I cannot access the portal or my exemption certificate?
a: Confirm your TIN login details, retry via a stable connection, then contact URA support if the certificate or status does not load.

q: Who can help with exemption questions?
a: URA support: toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000 or WhatsApp 0772 140 000.

q: What are Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs)?
a: Not-for-profit organisations independent of government that work for public benefit; funding often comes from donations, grants, and occasionally sales of goods or services.

q: Are NGOs required to register for taxes?
a: Yes. After registering with the National Bureau for NGOs, they must register with URA and obtain a Tax Identification Number (TIN) per NGO Act Section 29(1).

q: What are the TIN registration requirements for NGOs?
a: Certificate of incorporation by guarantee, Company Form 20, NGO certificate, and the NGO constitution.

q: How are NGOs registered for taxes?
a: Preferably online via the URA portal: download the non-individual TIN Excel template, complete mandatory fields, validate, upload, submit, and print the acknowledgement and form; then submit signed copies with attachments to URA. Offline help is available at URA service centres.

q: What income tax relief is available to NGOs?
a: Income tax exemption is available to NGOs undertaking charitable, educational, or religious activities whose objective is not for profit.

q: What does it mean for an NGO to have tax-exempt status?
a: It does not pay corporate income tax on donations and related-purpose income. Only NGOs exclusively pursuing not-for-profit purposes qualify, and exemption is granted after URA approval.

q: What makes an NGO eligible for income tax exemption?
a: It must be organised and operated solely for charitable, religious, or educational purposes; assets must be dedicated to those purposes in perpetuity; and no income or assets may benefit private persons such as directors or founders.

q: What documents support an application for income tax exemption?
a: Form DT 1015; certificate of incorporation (company limited by guarantee) and NGO registration; valid NGO permit; memorandum and articles/trust deed/constitution; list of subscribers/trustees with TINs; income tax returns for the prior 3 years; asset list; PAYE returns for last 6 months; tenancy/title; audited accounts for last 3 years; bank statements for last 3 years; confirmation letter from local authority/umbrella body; declaration; and any other relevant evidence.

q: What are the income tax exemption categories?
a: Charitable purposes (public welfare such as relief of the underprivileged, advancement of religion/education/science, social welfare), educational purposes (registered institutions providing education not for profit), and religious purposes (advancing a faith or belief).

q: What is the procedure for obtaining income tax exemption status?
a: Apply online to URA with supporting documents; URA reviews and, if satisfied, issues an exemption certificate. Once issued, the NGO is exempt for income tax but must continue routine filings and can be audited; if denied, its income is taxable.

q: What taxes are applicable to NGOs?
a: Corporate income tax applies unless an exemption ruling is granted. NGOs designated as withholding agents must withhold 6% on goods/services payments above UGX 1,000,000 and 6% on management/professional fees, remitting within 15 days after month-end. VAT applies on non-exempt goods/services; donations and grants are outside VAT scope; VAT on charitable expenses is not recoverable. PAYE must be withheld on employee earnings above UGX 235,000 per month at resident/non-resident rates and remitted monthly.

q: How is a tax-exempt NGO treated for withholding tax?
a: An income tax–exempt NGO also qualifies for WHT exemption on payments due to it from supplies to government or WHT agents and is exempt from WHT at importation.

q: Which NGOs are exempted from VAT?
a: Only NGOs gazetted in the First Schedule of the VAT Act as public international organizations are exempt on all expenditure; other NGOs pay VAT on non-exempt supplies.

q: Can a tax-exempt NGO earn business income without losing exemption?
a: Yes, but unrelated business income is taxable, and it must not become a substantial part of activities to avoid jeopardizing exempt status.

q: What other tax obligations do NGOs have?
a: File provisional and final income tax returns regardless of exemption, pay stamp duty on legal instruments, and comply with all general taxpayer obligations (e.g., PAYE, WHT, VAT where applicable).

q: Who must register for Income Tax and get a TIN?
a: Any person earning taxable income (individuals, companies, NGOs, partnerships) must register; individuals use NIN with ID documents, non-individuals need incorporation/registration documents and director TINs.

q: When is VAT registration compulsory?
a: When taxable turnover exceeds UGX 37.5m in any 3 consecutive months (UGX 150m annual). Apply within 20 days after the three-month period or at the start if future turnover will exceed the threshold.

q: Can a business register for VAT voluntarily?
a: Yes, below the threshold if it has a fixed place of business, proper books, can file reliably, and is fit-and-proper; public bodies doing business must register when they start.

q: What are key VAT obligations after registration?
a: Issue e-invoices, charge 18% on standard-rated supplies (0% for zero-rated, none on exempt), keep records, and file/pay monthly VAT returns within 15 days after month-end.

q: How is VAT input tax credited?
a: Keep original tax invoices (or certified copies) for local purchases and customs documents for imports; claims allowed within 6 months of invoice; only for business use and to support taxable supplies; cash refund only if credit exceeds UGX 10m, else carried forward.

q: What is Digital Service Tax?
a: A 5% tax on gross earnings of non-resident persons providing digital services to customers in Uganda.

q: Who must affix Digital Tax Stamps?
a: Manufacturers/importers of gazetted excisable goods (e.g., alcohol, tobacco, water, soda, sugar, cement, cooking oil, juices) must affix stamps before goods enter the market.

q: What is the presumptive (small business) regime?
a: Resident businesses with annual turnover above UGX 10m and not exceeding UGX 150m (excluding listed professional/utility/entertainment/construction services) pay presumptive tax based on gross turnover instead of formal accounts.

q: How is presumptive tax computed?
a: With records: 0.4% of turnover above UGX 10m up to 30m; 0.5% above 30m up to 50m; 0.6% above 50m up to 80m; 0.7% above 80m up to 150m. Without records: fixed UGX 80k (10–30m), 200k (30–50m), 400k (50–80m), 900k (80–150m). No expense deductions; tax is final.

q: What is the corporation tax rate?
a: 30% of chargeable income on resident companies’ worldwide income and non-resident companies’ Ugandan-source income.

q: How is rental income taxed?
a: Individuals: first UGX 2,820,000 exempt, remainder taxed at 12% with no deductions; non-resident individuals 15% on gross. Companies/non-individuals: 30% on chargeable rental income with allowable expenses capped at 50% of gross rental income.

q: What are PAYE rates for resident employees?
a: Monthly brackets: up to 235,000 nil; 235,000–335,000 at 10% of excess over 235,000; 335,000–410,000 at 10,000 + 20% of excess over 335,000; above 410,000 at 25,000 + 30% of excess over 410,000 plus an additional 10% on income above 10,000,000.

q: What are PAYE rates for non-resident employees?
a: Up to 335,000 taxed at 10%; 335,000–410,000 at 33,500 + 20% of excess over 335,000; above 410,000 at 48,500 + 30% of excess over 410,000 plus an additional 10% on income above 10,000,000.

q: What are employer obligations for PAYE?
a: Withhold correctly from liable employees, remit PAYE by the 15th of the following month, account monthly, and keep payroll records for 5 years; failure makes employer personally liable plus interest/penalties.

q: What withholding tax (WHT) rates apply to common payments?
a: 6% on resident payments for goods/services over UGX 1m by designated agents; 6% on resident management/professional fees; 15% on payments to non-resident contractors, professionals, entertainers/sportspersons; 15% on dividends/interest/royalties to non-residents; 10% on dividends from listed companies to residents; 10% on commissions to insurance/advertising/telecom/payment agents; 15% on betting winnings.

q: When is WHT due and how is it credited?
a: Agents must remit WHT within 15 days after month-end (or before payee leaves Uganda); unless final, withheld tax is a credit against the payee’s income tax for that year.

q: How is import WHT applied?
a: 6% on customs value for most imports unless the importer/supplier is exempt or has WHT relief; rates for customs duties and VAT still apply separately.

q: When is rental and income tax filing due?
a: Individuals: provisional rental return within 3 months from start of year (by 31 Sept), final within 6 months after year-end (by 31 Dec); companies: provisional within 6 months from start (by 31 Dec), final within 6 months after year-end.

q: What is the VAT registration penalty for late application?
a: Double the VAT due from the date registration should have occurred until actual registration.

q: How are NGOs and public bodies treated for VAT?
a: Public bodies engaging in business must register and charge VAT; supplies by employers to employees for no consideration are taxable at fair market value if the employer is a taxable person.

q: What is a small business for tax purposes?
a: A business with annual sales between UGX 10,000,000 and UGX 150,000,000 (about UGX 27,500+ per day).

q: What tax applies to small businesses?
a: The presumptive tax charged by URA on operators within the small-business turnover band.

q: Who pays this tax?
a: Owners of small businesses within the presumptive turnover range.

q: Does every business in that band pay presumptive tax?
a: No. Professionals such as medical, dental, engineering, accounting, and architectural practices (among others) are excluded from this tax.

q: What should I do after getting a TIN?
a: Create a URA portal account, log in with your TIN and default password, change it, and use the account to file returns, amend details, track payments, and other services.

q: Why is a URA portal account important?
a: It gives notifications on TIN activity, lets you file returns, follow payments, object/appeal, amend details, transfer vehicles, and appoint a clearing agent.

q: What are my core rights as a taxpayer?
a: Fair and consistent treatment; privacy/confidentiality; clear, timely information; reasons for decisions; timely service; right to object/appeal; to be heard with representation; notice before routine inspections; refunds processed per law.

q: What are my obligations?
a: Register, file accurate/timely returns and entries, pay correct tax on time, keep accurate records, quote TIN in dealings, avoid evasion/illegality, cooperate with authorized staff, disclose fully, comply with customs/quarantine rules, treat URA staff respectfully.

q: Why keep business records?
a: To prepare returns (avoid estimated assessments), monitor business/financials, track deductible expenses, and pay fair taxes; retain at least five years.

q: What return types exist?
a: Provisional (estimate for current year) and final (actual for past year); frequency depends on tax type—weekly (gaming), monthly (PAYE, WHT, VAT, excise, gaming), annual (income tax, partnerships, rental, presumptive).

q: When are returns and payments due?
a: Annual: provisional—last day of 3rd month (individual) or 6th month (company) with installments during year; final—within 6 months after year-end. Monthly: PAYE/WHT/VAT/excise/gaming/diplomatic VAT by 15th of following month. Weekly gaming: Wednesday following week. Payment is due same day as filing.

q: Can I get more time to file?
a: You may apply for an extension (up to 90 days total) with reasons, but payment due dates do not shift—interest still accrues on unpaid tax.

q: What happens if I file or pay late?
a: Late filing triggers penalties; late payment accrues interest at 2% per month until paid.

q: How can I pay?
a: Banks, mobile money, USSD *285#, VISA/MasterCard/AmEx/UnionPay, EFT/RTGS/SWIFT, cash, cheque, demand draft, POS.

q: Can I pay in installments?
a: Yes—apply to URA for permission to pay in installments.

q: What assessments can URA issue?
a: Estimated/default if you fail to file; advance assessment if there’s risk to collection before due; additional assessments when new info or fraud/gross neglect is found.

q: Can I object to an assessment?
a: Yes. You may lodge an objection if dissatisfied with an assessment.

q: Can my TIN be deactivated?
a: Yes, if you temporarily close business (can later reactivate) or if URA finds you no longer meet registration conditions.

q: Where can I get help?
a: URA portal and Touch Point; toll-free 0800 117 000 / 0800 217 000; WhatsApp 0772 140 000; email services@ura.go.ug; social channels (Facebook, X, TikTok, YouTube) and Taxman blog.

q: What is VAT?
a: An indirect tax on consumption, charged on value added to goods and services at each stage; applies to taxable supplies by a taxable person, imports (non-exempt), and imported services (non-exempt).

q: What are taxable, standard-rated, zero-rated, and exempt supplies?
a: Taxable supplies are non-exempt supplies made for consideration. Standard-rated attract 18%; zero-rated attract 0% (e.g., exports, locally made drugs/medicines, certain Ugandan cereals). Exempt supplies (Second Schedule) have no VAT and include health/life insurance, petroleum fuels, social welfare, education, financial services, passenger transport.

q: Who must register for VAT?
a: Anyone making taxable supplies whose sales exceed UGX 37.5m in any 3 consecutive months or UGX 150m in 12 months; public bodies carrying on business must register regardless of turnover.

q: Can I register voluntarily?
a: Yes, below the threshold if you have a fixed place of business, proper records, and are fit-and-proper.

q: How is VAT calculated (input vs output)?
a: Output VAT is VAT you charge on sales; input VAT is VAT you paid on taxable purchases/imports. If output > input, pay the difference; if input > output, you can claim (refund if > UGX 5m) or carry forward.

q: What if supply value isn’t clear?
a: Use fair market value at the time of supply (e.g., barter, gifts, own use).

q: What are obligations after VAT registration?
a: Charge VAT and issue tax invoices; register and use EFRIS for e-invoices/e-receipts; file VAT returns within 15 days after month-end (pre-filled via EFRIS); pay any VAT due within 15 days; maintain proper records.

q: How does EFRIS relate to VAT?
a: All VAT-registered taxpayers must issue e-invoices/e-receipts through EFRIS; they should also buy from suppliers who issue e-invoices when VAT applies. Non-VAT taxpayers may use EFRIS voluntarily (issuing e-receipts).

q: What is consideration?
a: Payment in money or kind (wholly or partly) for a taxable supply.

q: Who is a taxable person?
a: Anyone registered for VAT or required to be registered (individuals, partnerships, trusts, companies, government bodies, listed institutions).

q: What VAT rate applies to imports and imported services?
a: VAT applies to imports (unless exempt) and to imported services; the importer/receiver is liable.

q: When are VAT returns and payments due?
a: Within 15 days after the end of each month for VAT-registered persons.

q: What happens if I deal only in exempt supplies?
a: You do not register for VAT; VAT obligations apply only to standard/zero-rated taxable supplies.

q: What is whistleblowing to URA?
a: Reporting activities that may be illegal, unethical, or against URA policies/standards/regulations that harm revenue mobilization.

q: Who can be a whistleblower?
a: Any person or entity making a protected disclosure (public, contractors, applicants, employees of other entities). URA staff cannot whistleblow on revenue non-compliance due to their access.

q: Is there a reward for reporting?
a: Yes. If information leads to identification of unassessed tax/duty: 1% of the tax/duty assessed or UGX 15m (whichever is lower). If it leads to recovery: 5% of the tax/duty recovered or UGX 100m (whichever is lower).

q: How is a whistleblower protected?
a: Identity protected under the Whistleblowers Act against victimization, court action, and with possible state protection; URA may discipline staff who retaliate; confidentiality maintained, and disclosure of identity only if necessary for investigation after informing the whistleblower.

q: How can I submit a disclosure?
a: Orally or in writing using any ICT channel. Provide as much detail as possible.

q: What details should a disclosure include?
a: Your name/address/occupation; nature of the impropriety; names/details of persons involved; time/place; witnesses’ details; whether you reported before and to whom; and if employment-related, whether you remain employed.

q: Can URA staff retaliate against whistleblowers?
a: No. Retaliation can trigger disciplinary proceedings; unwarranted confidentiality breaches may also lead to discipline.

q: What is withholding tax (WHT)?
a: An income tax withheld at source by a withholding agent when paying a payee, then remitted to URA in advance.

q: Who can be a withholding agent?
a: A person legally obliged to withhold—either designated in a gazette notice or making a payment subject to WHT by law.

q: What kinds of WHT exist?
a: Final WHT (satisfies tax on that income; no further return/tax, no deductions/refunds) and creditable WHT (advance tax credit offset against final liability).

q: Key resident PAYE (employment) rates?
a: Residents monthly: 0–235k nil; 235–335k 10% of excess; 335–410k 10k + 20% of excess; above 410k 25k + 30% of excess + extra 10% on income over 10m. Non-resident: up to 335k at 10%; 335–410k 33.5k + 20% excess; above 410k 48.5k + 30% excess + extra 10% over 10m.

q: Common WHT rates on payments?
a: 6% goods/services to designated agents over UGX 1m; 6% resident management/professional fees; 15% betting winnings; 6% import WHT on customs value (unless exempt); 15% interest to residents (with exclusions/final for T-bills/bonds to individuals/retirement funds/expected orgs); 15% dividends to residents (10% for listed to residents; resident individuals’ dividend WHT is final); 15% on non-resident dividends/interest/royalties/rent/management charges; 15% on non-resident service contracts; 10% reinsurance premiums to non-residents; 10% commissions to insurance/advertising agents; 10% commissions to mobile money dealers (final).

q: When must WHT be remitted?
a: Within 15 days after month-end; for non-resident entertainers/sports, within 5 days of performance or before departure, whichever is earlier.

q: What records must agents keep?
a: Payment and WHT records for 5 years and make them available to URA.

q: Consequences of failing to withhold/remit?
a: Agent is personally liable for the tax that should have been withheld; can recover from payee later.

q: Do amounts under the 1m threshold escape WHT on contracts?
a: No—if total contract payments exceed UGX 1m, WHT applies to any part payments once aggregated over the threshold.

q: Is import WHT always due?
a: Yes at 6% on customs value unless importer/supplier is exempt or has WHT relief.

q: Do PAYE and WHT returns share the same deadline?
a: Yes—file and pay by the 15th of the following month.
